title: How I Write A Blog Article
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In response to reader curiosity, Linsin walks through his week-long process for writing a single SCM article, from Saturday topic selection through the following Saturday's publish button. He describes choosing topics by weighing reader requests, time of year, and the need to balance new subscribers against long-time readers, then mentally visualizing the article for a day before writing a full draft in one sitting on Sunday. The rest of the week is spent revising: Monday and Tuesday for content and structure, Wednesday for grammar and word choice, Thursday for reading aloud and pacing, and Friday for formatting it in WordPress, adding links and an image, and running it through Grammarly. Finally, his wife — also a teacher and his reader of twelve years — reviews every article before it's published the following Saturday morning. The piece offers a candid look at the discipline behind a blog many readers assume is dashed off quickly.
points: Article topics are chosen weekly by weighing reader requests, seasonal relevance, and the need to serve both new and longtime subscribers.
A full first draft is written in one sitting after a day of mental visualization, without editing while writing.
Revision is spread across the week: content and structure (Mon/Tue), grammar and word choice (Wed), read-aloud pacing (Thu), and WordPress formatting plus Grammarly (Fri).
Every article is reviewed by his wife, also a teacher, before it goes live on Saturday morning.
quotes: The truth is, it’s a lot of work that begins a week before hitting the publish button on Saturday morning.
I view SCM as a continuing education in effective classroom management, so I’m cognizant of the need to continually revisit previous themes.
Once I settle on a topic, I’ll spend 15-20 minutes writing the article in my head.
I usually spend one to two hours working on Sunday. I’ll pour my visualizations out onto the page and try my darnedest not to do any editing.
Finally, the article is ready for the big cheese, my wife, to read. She is also a teacher and has read everything I’ve written for the past 12 years.
On Saturday morning, I’ll read it aloud a couple more times, take a deep breath, and then hit “publish.
